## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

As someone who resides in Virginia, I am located near states with bad air pollution. Additionally, the east coast in general has more air pollution then the west coast.

raw_comment:
Notice: I notice that California, who is among the eight states with the greatest air pollution deaths, has its air pollution coming almost entirely from in-state sources. Also, the western states (excluding the three states on the coast) all have a very minimal number of air pollution deaths. Lastly, I was surprised to see that the majority of the air pollution related deaths in the country comes from the eastern side of the country, specifically from the countries between Ohio and Connecticut.

Wonder: I wonder what in-state factor causes the air pollution in California to be so dangerous. What out-of-state factors impact the eastern states with the greatest air pollution? In addition, I'm curious to know why the two states next to California, Nevada and Arizona, have such low air pollution death rates compared to California.

Impact on my Community: The quality of air on the east coast directly impacts me and my community. Virginia is right on the border of the cluster of states with the greatest number of air pollution related deaths. It is also important to note that Virginia does not have the best air quality either, and definitely has much room for improvement.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
Notice: Midwestern states have many less deaths compared to more built up states near the coat like New York or California. Some states are very high in air pollution deaths, like California, New York, and Illinois. Lot's of midwestern state's air pollution deaths are from out of state pollution, while coastal and large state deaths are more from instate pollution.

Wonder: When analyzing this, I was thinking to myself, how does airflow and wind across the US affect the other states which don't really produce much air pollution. It would be interesting to overlay the in-out-of-state graph on top of a graph of the airflow/wind currents on the US. Also, are the deaths in the very high death states due to large cities, like Los Angeles, New York City, or Chicago?

Impact: To me, this indicates that pollution is being a big problem, with palpable consequences, including my own state.

|---|---|---|

raw_comment:
I noticed that states with higher populations and larger cities have more premature deaths than states with lower population. Also, most of the mountain states (Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming), have significantly fewer deaths due to air pollution compared to other states. 

I wonder why Delaware and South Dakota have so many deaths from out of state. I also wonder why the number of deaths from the states near California are so low, but other states with high numbers of death are surrounded by states with moderate to high numbers of death.

This data impacts communities in several ways. For one, it informs on how many precautions the community should take in regards to air pollution. It informs scientists in the area of the level of air pollution, which might have an impact on what they are studying. It informs hospitals and clinics how many people that treat air pollution damage should be staffed, and how much resources they need in order to treat the damage. It also informs environmental regulators of whether or not their regulations are efficient in decreasing deaths due to air pollution.

A catchy headline for this graph might be "Air Pollution: A Hidden Killer"

raw_comment:
In the first map, I noticed that states that are more densely populated tend to have more air pollution, perhaps because there are more people that need to be provided with power, heating, and transportation. However in the second map, Western and southern states are mostly impacted by in-state pollution, whereas the middle and eastern coast states are mainly affected by pollution from neighboring states.

I wonder why middle and eastern states are more likely to be affected by pollution from out of state, or what helps them manage in-state pollution better than western states.

The data displayed in the maps reflect the actual amount of pollution in the U.S. It is important for the community to study why air pollution has become an increasing issue in some states and how actions can be put in place to prevent pollution from developing. Excess amounts of air pollution can lead to other environmental problems, such as global warming and climate change.

Map 1 exhibits the amount of deaths related to air pollution in each state. Map 2 displays whether the pollution for each state comes from surrounding states or within the state.

raw_comment:
Notice:
I notice that for the first map, there is a lot of air pollution in heavily populated states, particularly California, Illinois, Ohio, and the New England area. From the second map, I notice that in heavily populated states, the majority of air pollution - related deaths are in-state, while in less densely populated areas, the majority of air pollution - related deaths are out-of-state.

Wonder:
I wonder why the air pollution death rate in Florida is low for the first graph. I also wonder why the previously high rate for air pollution death rate in the New England area for the first graph is low in the second graph on where most deaths are located. 

Impact:
Since this is real data, I can see the overwhelming effects of air pollution. I find that statistics and real numbers are more convincing than just words, so implementing these graphs and statistics would help me and my community realize the detrimental effects of air pollution across the country. 

Main Idea:
These maps show the places that air pollution has affected the most, and places where it is relatively better. Using this data and information, stronger efforts can be put towards solving the immense problem of air pollution. A catchy title to bring awareness to the results of this article would be "The unseen epidemic: Air Pollution"

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |

| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

I Noticed: I noticed that states with higher populations and more specifically higher population densities, tended to have a higher amount of deaths associated with air pollution. The further we move from big population hubs the lower the amount of deaths which is found in less populated states such as Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Montana. What I also noticed was that states with lower populations were more affected by states with larger populations in terms of out of state pollution

raw_comment:
1. I notice that states with a higher population tend to have more air pollution deaths because this graph shows a darker purple when indicating more deaths. These higher population states include New York, California, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, and New Jersey. It is also apparent that most of these states are on the coastline, and that there tend to be fewer air pollution deaths in more of central America.  

2. I wonder why most of the eastern states tend to have a higher number of air pollution deaths than states more to the western side of the United States. I also wonder why South Dakota has the most out-of-state pollution in the entire United States. 

3. This graph has an impact on me and my community because it is important to understand air pollution and its impact on society such as these death rates. In the future, it will only get worse and it is important to try my best to limit this as much as possible.

raw_comment:
- What do you notice?

I notice that border/coastal states, especially ones that are highly populated, tend to have a lot of deaths due to air pollution. I also notice that South Dakota has the most deaths form out of state air pollution compared to all of the other 50 states.

- What do you wonder?

I know that Illinois is quite populated, yet it's not one of the border states. So, this makes me wonder if air population is more due to a states' location or population? I also wonder why South Dakota has the most deaths due to out of state air pollution. Is there a backstory behind it? 

- What impact does this have on you and your community?

Air pollution has a major impact on my community and even the world because it's causing a great environmental impact, like global warming. These changes can cause great harm to our environment, air, and other living beings. Air is crucial for us to live, so it's important to prioritize it's cleanliness and quality. 

- What’s going on in these maps? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.

These graphs show the number of deaths due to air pollution within a state from it's own pollution and out of state pollution. A catchy headline that captures the map's main ideas would be "The Air that Kills".

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
Notice: I notice that bigger states, like California, Texas, and Florida all have more in-state deaths. I also notice that the Mid/Midwest states don't really have a lot of in state pollution deaths, but mainly out of state deaths.

Wonder: I wonder why California and South Dakota have so many in state deaths. I also am curious why Delaware has the most deaths out of any state. Why do some states get more in-state air population while others get a lot more out-of-state.

Impact: Knowing the air pollution deaths and whether it is in state or out of state is important. Acknowledging how your state is doing in regards to air-pollution deaths will help keep you safe, and tell you whether you need to start spreading awareness or taking safety protocols about this pollution crisis.

Headline: The map of the United States is showing the amount of air pollution in each state. If the color is blue, the pollution is from in-state and orange is from out-of-state. The darker the color, the more deaths from pollution.

A catchy headline would be "Air Pollution is now affecting people not only in-state, but out-of-state as well"

raw_comment:
Notice: I noticed that states on both coasts tend to have higher death rates from air pollution, and that manufacturing powerhouses also tend to have higher premature death rates from air pollution. 

Wonder: I wonder why South Dakota has so much out of state air pollution coming in. Which states is that coming from? How do we know where air pollution is coming from in general?

Impact: It's important to understand the effect of air pollution on my community, and what the general death rate is. This knowledge is also important for lawmakers in my community, in order to create legislation to limit air pollution.

Headline: How Air Pollution from Surrounding States Can Directly Impact Citizens

raw_comment:
1. After looking closely at the 2 graphs, I noticed that number of air pollution related deaths usually corresponds with the population of a state. For example, New York has a high population, and therefore has a higher death rate. A state like Utah, however, has a less population rate and therefore has a lower death rate. I also noticed that states on the coastline tend to have more in-state deaths.

2.  Something that I wonder about this graph is why does a highly populated state like New York have more out of state air pollution when it is so highly populated, and is known for its many buildings and transportation, which contribute to in-state pollution?

3.  Pollution has a high impact on humans and our communities. It impacts our health as well as other living beings' health as well. It also contributes to global warming and is overall negative for the environment.

4. These 2 maps show a connection between population and  pollution. It also shows that for some states, the majority of air pollution related deaths aren't even from in-state, and that pollution can spread to other states as well. A catchy title for this could be "Pollution has no Boundaries; Affecting American Lives from Out of State."

raw_comment:
1. After looking closely at the 2 graphs, I noticed that number of air pollution related deaths usually corresponds with the population of a state. For example, New York has a high population, and therefore has a higher death rate. A state like Utah, however, has a less population rate and therefore has a lower death rate. I also noticed that states on the coastline tend to have more in-state deaths.

2.  Something that I wonder about this graph is why does a highly populated state like New York have more out of state air pollution when it is so highly populated, and is known for its many buildings and transportation, which contribute to in-state pollution?

3.  Pollution has a high impact on humans and our communities. It impacts our health as well as other living beings' health as well. It also contributes to global warming and is overall negative for the environment.

4. These 2 maps show a connection between population and  pollution. It also shows that for some states, the majority of air pollution related deaths aren't even from in-state, and that pollution can spread to other states as well. A catchy title for this could be "Pollution has no Boundaries; Affecting American Lives from Out of State."

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I've noticed that in the first graph, near the northeast more people are dying from air pollution, but in the second graph, it shows that the people dying are more due to out of state pollution. This is true especially in Delaware. It also shows that California produces the most in state death rate and the west often produces more pollution (not confirmed but the graph implies it).

What do you wonder?
I wonder how and where the pollution originates. Since a lot of people die near the northeast but they don't produce that much pollution, where does it come from? Maybe it comes from the states near it with blue? Or could it possibly have traveled all the way from the west to the east?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
The impact it has could possibly affect our families and friends. It applies more on the animals since they might not have gotten used to pollution. This might weaken the rates of oxygen as well and eventually cause more deaths. This then heats up the atmosphere and causes the world to go out of balance.

What’s going on in these maps? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.
Most states in the west produce there own pollution and cause there own deaths while the people in the northeast has some factories pollution themselves and most spreading it to others. Also the middle-west has almost no deaths.
Headline : Air Pollution - The Deadly Toxin

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

1. I noticed that the first graph clearly illustrates that more premature deaths from air pollution occur in the eastern half of the U.S. On the other hand, the second graph shows that most of the deaths in the eastern half are because of air pollution that comes from out of state, while the western half has more deaths caused by in state pollution. raw_comment:
From looking at the two graphs in the New York Times article, I noticed that the eastern side of the country, mainly the coast, has way more air pollution deaths than the western side of the country. I think that this makes sense, as my knowledge tells me that there are a lot more cities and urban areas on the eastern side of the country compared to the western side. This would cause people living in these urban areas to consume more air pollution due to vehicles and factories, therefore driving the death rates up. Along with that, I wonder why the deaths on the western side of the country are more instate, while the western side is mainly due to out of state pollution. An idea that I have for this occurrence is that foreign pollution could be causing more out of state pollution deaths in the east coast. I remember learning about air currents a while ago, and I remember that the east coast is right in the middle of the stream running from China and other parts of Asia. This could definitely bring over lots of pollution.
	This therefore would greatly impact our community. This is because we are living right on the east coast, and would be in the middle of any pollution coming from foriegn continents. This is reflected in the graph, as it shows that the majority of pollution related deaths in New Hampshire are mainly from out of state pollution. A headline I would give these graphs is, “Pollution Deaths by State”.

raw_comment:
"Air Pollution Death: How Can We Minimize IT Before It's Too Late?"


I noticed that states with large cities and urban areas appear to have higher air pollution rates. For comparison to the lower graph, it is interesting to see some of these populations experience higher premature death rates due to pollution outside of states such as New York.

I wonder why the midwest has such low death rates compared to the rest of the map. I assume it is because these urban areas are more prone to pollution by car and other machinery, as well as factories. However, I wonder how a place like California could be so dense in air pollution without effecting it's neighboring states to the slightest?


This impacts my community, and honestly, I oblivious to the half of it. I had no idea how high my home state, New Hampshire, landed in comparison to other states on this graph. I had no idea that states of New England were the states with the most deaths per 10,000 residents. I have lots of family in the Northeast as well and this makes me nervous for them. I think that this important issue could be slipping over many peoples' noses, just as it did mine.

raw_comment:
I see that the first graph is a map of all the mainland US states and how many air pollution deaths there are per 10,000 residents. The average amount of deaths per 10,000 people is 2.5 with 10 states with only 1 death, 12 states with 2, 18 states with 3, and 8 states with 4. The next graph shows us what percentage of the mainland states’ air pollution deaths are from in or out of state air pollution. 18 states have most deaths attributed to in state pollution whereas 30 states have most deaths attributed to out of state pollution.

I wonder where New York’s out of state pollution comes from since I thought New York was a big producer of air pollution.

While this is a pretty big deal, it’s almost natural for this to happen because of our heavy reliance on fossil fuels for electricity and transportation. It’s saddening, but also something I’d expect to see.

“Death in the Air”

raw_comment:
I notice that the more urban areas such as New York and California tend to have worse air quality and therefore more deaths per 10,000 people than more rural states such as Montana or Wyoming. I would assume this would be due to the higher production rates taking place in the industrialized areas, compared to the more nature-focused rural states.

I wonder how Hawaii and Alaska would compare to these states. I would imagine since Alaska is a predominantly uninhabited land, their numbers would be extremely low, but I would imagine it would be a different story for Hawaii. Though Hawaii is a state often associated with nature and beauty, there is the big city of Honolulu and the air pollution that comes from the eruptions of volcanoes.

Though I don’t walk out the door and worry about the quality of air around me in New Hampshire, my state still sees about two deaths per 10,000 people due to air pollution. I would imagine based on the second graph that some of this pollution comes from Massachusetts, and I think a stronger effort needs to be made to move towards more renewable and forgiving energy sources.

These graphs depict the deaths that are caused by air pollution per 10,000 people on a state by state basis and also shows whether or not that pollution is coming from in or out of state.
 
Catchy Headline: Pollution: The Silent Killer

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
These graphs pose a pressing topic in today's society. To put it simply they show air pollution deaths across the US. I notice that these deaths are more centered around heavily populated areas such as California and New York.
2. What do you wonder?
These graphs make me wonder what the US is currently doing to protect against these deaths. Are there any works in place under the Biden administration to help with this cause?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
I was relatively surprised to see that my state (New Hampshire) lies in the upper third of the spectrum for the first graph. I usually don’t consider my state to be polluted. This impacts me because it shows me that there really is a problem within my community which I otherwise would not have known about.
4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Pollution by population, or Industry?

raw_comment:
What I first noticed after taking a glance at the graphs is how states which hold a larger population with large cities tended to have more air pollution. This however did not stand as a surprise to me because with such populated areas in states such as New York and California, the cities like Los Angeles and New York City run rampant with pollution. This also stands as no surprise because states like California, Ohio, and Illinois all are known for their many factories.

I mainly wonder what contributes most to the air pollution in the dark purple states. As factories definitely play a very large role, I would assume cars and other gas using machinery also contribute. As it is known, with the larger population of people, the more cars would be used, causing the greenhouse gas emissions from them to affect the atmosphere.

As I live in New Hampshire, I had no idea that my state was on the higher end of this graph. We as a state have between two and three air pollution deaths per 10,000 citizens. At first, I didn’t believe this was a lot, but when put in proportion to our state population of 1.36 million, there are around 272 to 408 citizens dying every year from it.

These pair of graphs highlight the deaths due to air pollution per each state in the United States. “What your states air pollution means.”

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

I notice that the states with bigger populations such as California and New York both have higher air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents. I wonder how much of a factor population plays in the amount of pollution?
I wonder why the Eastern side of the US has more out of state deaths?

4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
These graphs are showing the deaths per air pollution by state per 10,000 people.
“Be Careful What You Breathe”

1. I notice that states that generally have a higher population have more pollution deaths in general. The pollution doesn’t seem to spread much out of the state borders, as evident by the mass amounts of pollution deaths in California and the relatively low deaths in neighboring states like Nevada and Arizona.  In contrast to this, much of the northeast and eastern seaboard have pollution death rates of 2 or higher/10,000.
2. I wonder what state legislature has to do with the pollution deaths.  Do some states protect their workers more than others, and does that result in less deaths?  In addition to this, I’m also curious about the out-of-state deaths, especially in the northeast.  Nearly every northeast state has more deaths due to out-of-state pollution, besides Ma. and Pa.  
3. Living in the northeast, this has a major impact on my life and those around me.  As evident by the first graph, the northeast region has the most deaths/10,000 caused by pollution in the country.  This could have effects on those who are more susceptible to illness or other side effects from pollution, as well as my own long-term health.  
4. “The Side Effects of Economic Prosperity”

1. What do you notice?

I wonder why California is the only state west of the Mississippi River that has 3+ deaths per 10,000 residents due to air pollution. Also, I wonder why the states bordering the great lakes are so bad in this department.

“California Love?”

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

I noticed that high density states such as California, Illinois, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Connecticut and New York have the highest dates from air pollution.
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why these specific states have more deaths by air pollution than other states. I also wonder why the midwest has such low death rates compared to the rest of the map. 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts all of us because air pollution is getting worse everyday and our lives are at risk if we don't improve our ways of living and clean our earth from all kinds of pollution.
4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
The graph shows which states have the most premature deaths from air pollution. A catchy headline could be "The Air Of Death"

raw_comment:
1. The highest category of shading is three or more deaths per 10,000 due to air pollution. 3 out of 10,000 may not seem like a lot, but it definitely scales up when you have states with large populations such as New York and Pennsylvania. That region of the country, (around the Northeast and Midwest), seems to have the highest rates of deaths due to air pollution outside of California. These areas tend to have higher populations and are traditionally more reliant on industry. 
The second display shows whether each state’s air pollution deaths are from air pollution coming from out of state or within the state. There are some pockets of the country that lean one way or the other, but there isn’t a clear east coast/west coast divide like there was in the other map.
2. For the second display, I wonder how they determine which air pollution deaths are caused by air pollution from out of state. 
3. I am from the Northeast. It seems like the Northeast, and the East Coast in general, have a higher rate of air pollution deaths than the rest of the country. I have asthma so this is probably good information for me to know personally. 
4. The first map shows that certain areas of the country tend to have greater amounts of deaths due to air pollution. The second shows which pockets of the country have air pollution deaths from out of state pollution and which from in state pollution.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that the midwest states have the least amount of air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents. I also noticed that CA, Ohio, NY, PA, Conn, Maryland, and NJ all have the highest amounts of air pollution deaths per 10,000 people. New York and California don’t surprise me much because they both have big cities within them. I notice that in the second graph California is the only dark state meaning it has a lot of in state air pollution deaths. I also notice that Delaware has the most out of state air pollution deaths. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder if a more populated area would create more air polluted deaths because more people are driving around or maybe more people have a chance to die from it. I also wonder why Florida doesn’t have high air pollution deaths because it has a high population and many cities.
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This impacts my community because New Hampshire is the second to darkest purple shade meaning it is one of the higher deaths by air pollution. raw_comment: In the top graph, I notice the higher rates of death from air pollution occur in higher populated states. Five of the eight states with a rate of 3 deaths/10,000 residents are in the top 10 highest populated states. However, highly-populated Texas and Florida have a rate comparable to Vermont, the second-lowest populated state. To understand this seeming contradiction, factors like population density and industrial conditions should be considered. In the bottom graph, I notice deaths are more frequently caused by in-state sources along the West Coast and out-of-state on the East Coast. I wonder what impact the pandemic would have on this data. If we created new graphs, would air pollution-related deaths be lower due to our nation’s lockdown? I also wonder why so many of South Dakota’s deaths come from out-of-state sources. Unlike New Hampshire, its neighboring states have low air pollution death rates, so what's causing this? This impacts my community because I live in NH which has a relatively high air pollution death rate. It's something we need to be aware of as everyone's health is put at risk. We also have the highest deaths caused by out-of-state sources. Since we're surrounded by states with some of the highest air pollution death rates, this isn't surprising, but rather makes me wonder how we could prevent it. The graphs show the air pollution death rate in the US and whether the sources are in-state or out-of-state. "Air Pollution Is Not Only Harmful but Deadly."

raw_comment:
I noticed from the first graph that California, Illinois, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and New York are some of the states that have the highest rate of premature deaths from combustion-related air pollution. I also noticed that states in the midwest have the least amount of air pollution related deaths. From looking at the second graph, I noticed that California has the highest amount of air pollution related deaths, and most of their deaths are caused by in-state pollution. On the other hand, New York is one of the states with the most air pollution deaths, but the majority of the pollution is coming from other states. Lastly, Delaware’s air pollution is caused almost all from out of state.  
 
I wonder how much population density plays a factor in the air pollution deaths? I also wonder why bigger states like Texas and Florida don’t have as many air pollution deaths as California does?
 
By looking at the first graph, New Hampshire is in the top 75% for the highest amount of air pollution deaths. This is concerning because our state has a large number of deaths caused by air pollution, which is something we can somewhat control. Most of New Hampshire’s pollution is from other surrounding states, like Massachusetts, so although we can’t help that, there are small and simple ways individuals can contribute to decreasing air pollution around them.

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

After looking at the second graph I noticed that many of the air pollution deaths in the east was from out of state, where in California and more states to the west, it is mostly in-state.
I wonder why it is that in the west coast and midwest the deaths are mostly from in-state air pollution, whereas the east is mostly out of state. I also wonder where the out of state air pollution is coming from, in other words what state is polluting their neighbor states.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that states with large, population-dense cities such as Chicago, Illinois tend to have more air pollution deaths. The opposite is also true, with sparse, rural states such as North Dakota having fewer air pollution deaths. I also noticed that California has the most in-state deaths while South Dakota and especially Delaware have the more out-of-state deaths. 
2. I wonder why South Dakota in particular has such a high proportion of out-of-state deaths compared to similar states with fewer air pollution deaths. It definitely sticks out among states surrounding it such as Minnesota and North Dakota, and it seems unclear where this pollution is coming from. It would be good to conduct a statistical analysis to see whether this abnormally high proportion is caused by a specific factor or just chance. 
3. My home state, New Hampshire, is on the higher side when it comes to deaths by air pollution. Most of these deaths are caused by air pollution from out of state, which makes sense as we’re close to population-dense states such as New York and Massachusetts. This impacts my community because even if we reduce our own air pollution, deaths may not go down unless the states around us follow suit. 
4. This pair of graphs highlights the impact of urban, population-dense states on the places around them—rural communities can be affected from the pollution produced elsewhere. A title could be: “Who is Breathing Your Air?”

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the first graph clearly illustrates that more premature deaths from air pollution occur in the eastern half of the U.S. On the other hand, the second graph shows that most of the deaths in the eastern half are because of air pollution that comes from out of state, while the western half has more deaths caused by in state pollution. I also noticed and was surprised that New Hampshire's premature deaths from air pollution was surprisingly high. 

2. When looking at the second graph, I wonder what states are polluting the other states and causing the most air pollution deaths?
I also wonder how the U.S. pollution affects neighboring countries?

3. This impacts my community and I because I never thought pollution was an issue in New Hampshire or affecting our lives. The graphs show that we need states around us to reduce their pollution to help our community as well.

4. The graphs show how pollution is causing premature deaths within our states and how states are affecting each other's air pollution.
"Death Looming Around Us"

raw_comment:
In the first graph, I notice that the majority of the southwestern states, Utah, Colorado, Arizona, etc have relatively low rates for premature deaths due to air pollution. I noticed that the states with large populations have higher rates for premature deaths due to air pollution. In the second graph, I noticed that the states in the southwest and along the west coast have higher rates of death due to air pollution from in state sources, such as California and Washington. I also noticed that the majority of the midwestern states and many northeastern states had the majority of air pollution coming from out of state sources. 
 I wonder what the sources of air pollution are that are causing states along the west coast to have high death rates. I wonder what role population size plays in the death rate and the source of the air pollution?
New Hampshire has a relatively high air pollution death rate in comparison to other states. The majority of air pollution is coming from out of state sources. If we do not take action to work to lessen the air pollution in our community and across the country, there will be serious issues in the future. 
The first graph, is analyzing the number of deaths per 10,000 residents due to air pollution for each state in the US. The second graph is showing the source of the air pollution in each state, the scale shows if the air pollution comes from out of state sources or in state sources.

raw_comment:
What I notice at first glance is that the more populous states have more air pollution. This is honestly no surprise to me because a state with more population will no doubt have more people using stuff that produces air pollution. I also notice California has a LOT of air pollution. This could be due to the fact that factories are mostly located in California.

I wonder how much air pollution we really produce, and what’s producing it? Farming will use a lot of gas which can cause more air pollution, but I notice that small states that are typically populated with farmers have a lot fewer deaths. But this could once again be contributed to the population. California will use a lot due to their population, and more population means more cars. It really makes you wonder what causes all these deaths?

I live in North Carolina, so as a resident, 2 people per 10,000 people are dying of air pollution. The only problem is that there is no real solution for this. We cannot completely eliminate any of the everyday things that produce air pollution, such as driving a car, because people need to get to work safely and quickly.

Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
1) At first glance I noticed that New Hampshire was surprisingly high as to deaths per 10,000 residents. However after observing the second graph I noticed that most pollutants in New Hampshire are from out of state sources. Unsurprisingly I also observed that New York and Massachusetts had high numbers of deaths per 10,000 residents. That being said I was then surprised when I observed the second graph and saw that the majority of pollutants in those states come from out of state sources. 

2) I wonder what states cause New Hampshire to have two deaths per 10,000 residents and if those states are New York and Massachusetts, why those pollutants do not evenly affect Vermont as they have fewer deaths per 10,000 then  New Hampshire despite being right next to it. 

3) This impacts myself and my community as New Hampshire is shown to have two deaths per 10,000 and that the majority of pollutants causing these deaths are from out of state. It shows that even if we as a state reduced our pollutants, people would still die due to the actions of others. 

4) These graphs show the number of deaths per 10,000 residents due to air pollution and then go further in depth and show the deaths due to air pollution from either in state or out of state. 
 
A possible headline could be, Air Pollution: The Silent Killer

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

raw_comment:
I notice that the states with the greatest rate of premature deaths from combustion-related air pollution are California, Illinois, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Maryland, New Jersey, Connecticut, and New York. The Mid-West region has the lowest rate. States like Utah, Colorado, and others are light purple. It’s interesting to see that California, a heavily populated state has a higher rate of premature deaths than other heavily populated states like Texas and Florida. The population must not be a factor in the rate of premature deaths from air pollution. On the second graph, I noticed that the West Coast has a lot of states that have air pollution caused by in-state. States around Missouri have the opposite problem. California is the darkest blue state, meaning it receives the most in-state pollution. 
With the first graph, I wonder why California has a larger rate of premature deaths than states like Florida or Texas. Florida and Texas are also heavily populated states but have way fewer premature deaths than California. 
New Hampshire has a high rate of premature deaths from combustion-related air pollution. This is unsafe and threatens everyone’s health within New Hampshire. Most of these deaths are being caused by out-of-state pollution. Surrounding states are affecting the air quality not just in New Hampshire but across the country.
A catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea is “What Kind of Air are You Breathing?”.

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
In the first graph, I noticed that California, Illinois, and New York are some of the states with the greatest number of premature deaths caused by air pollution. These states all have large populations. In the second graph, I noticed that most of the states on the west coast have deaths caused by air pollution caused by in-state sources. 
 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why California has more premature deaths caused by air pollution than other states with large populations, like Texas and Florida. I wonder how much population density factors into these deaths. I wonder why air-pollution causing deaths on the west coast is caused in-state.

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
New Hampshire has a high number of deaths caused by air pollution and is close in proximity to other states with even higher death tolls. New Hampshire’s air-pollution is also mostly from out-of-state sources. This is definitely something that everyone in my community/state should be aware of. Our country greatly contributes to air pollution and we should be more conscious of our contribution to pollution.
 
4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
“Air Pollution Contribution Revolution”

raw_comment:
1. From the top graph, I noticed that states with higher population densities (California and New England states) tend to experience more deaths due to air pollution. From the bottom graph, I noticed that some states with more air pollution-related deaths tend to have these deaths due to out-of-state sources. However, the number of in and out-of-state pollution sources is fairly evenly distributed. There seems to be a higher occurrence of in-state pollution sources on the West coast compared to the East coast. 

2. The first thing I wonder is why neither Alaska nor Hawaii is on these maps, as it would be interesting to know their stats. I wonder why there are so many more in-state pollution sources on the West coast, as I would have thought pollution emissions among the two coasts are fairly similar. I also wonder what the main sources of in and out-of-state pollution are. 

3. This affects my community as I live in New Hampshire which has a moderate amount of air pollution-related deaths, meaning the health of those around me is in danger. The bottom map also tells me that much of this pollution comes from out-of-state sources. It would be interesting to find out what my community is doing to try and combat these pollution sources.

4. These graphs show the number of air pollution-related deaths in each state and whether they are caused by in-state or out-of-state sources.
Headline: "Danger in the Air: Pollution-Related Deaths Across the United States."

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
In the first graph that shows premature deaths in each state due to air pollution I see that states including California, Illinois, Ohio, etc. are all in the darker side. Those states have the big populations than others so that could be a factor of why the deaths are high. Texas has a lighter color although its big population. A likely reason why states like these which have huge populations are on the lighter side may be because of the amount of factories there are. The more factories/companies that cause air pollution may be lower in those states than in California and New York so that is why Texas and Florida are on the lighter side. In the second graph we can see that there are more deaths due to in state pollution than out of state

I wonder why states that border or are near the big states do not have the same impact as the state it borders with such percentages. I would think that these states that border the more impacted states would be in a darker color since air is a factor that carries the polluted air, so I would wonder why those states aren’t affected as much as they should be

This impacts my community by showing that there is a problem with air pollution in the states. I live in New Hampshire where the numbers aren’t as high as the other ones but it can still affect my community later on in life. There are ways to prevent or help to reverse them but that takes a lot of time and work to do so. It may affect us later 

The Slow Killer in the US, Air Pollution

I notice that the the more populated states have more population deaths like California, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, etc. Also notice that Hawaii and Alaska are not on this map of the United States.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I notice that in the graph showing the rate of premature deaths from air pollution is much higher in that of states with a larger population. In New York, California and Illinois, I noticed that they are have larger populations and deaths from pollution than that of others.
 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why the west has less deaths from air pollution than that of others. I assume that this is because states like Utah, Wyoming, and Colorado are not as densely populated than that of California, Illinois, and New York that all contain major cities, but I still wonder if there can be some other correlation as to why this is the case.
 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This has an impact on me and my community, as this is something that the community could take steps towards combating. Yes, I don’t live in an area where this is necessarily a larger issue, unlike the constant haze of air pollution in LA, but I still think we should always be working to better ourselves as a community, and we can take simple steps to better the environment we live in.
 
4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Pollution in the air? Or in our actions?

raw_comment:
1. In the first graph, I notice that the rate of premature deaths from combustion-related air pollution is higher in states with larger populations. For example, New York, California, and Illinois all have larger populations and higher pollution-related death rates than Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho. In the second graph, I notice that states along the West Coast generally have deaths due to in-state air pollution sources while states along the East Coast generally have deaths due to out-of-state air pollution sources. 

2. I wonder what the main source of air pollution is in each of these states. Does most of the air pollution come from car exhaust, electricity generation, or a different source? Do the sources differ from state to state?

3. This impacts my community because New Hampshire has a generally high air-pollution-death rate compared to other states. In addition, several of New Hampshire’s neighboring states also have high air-pollution-death rates, and most of New Hampshire’s air pollution is coming from sources in these other states. If the air quality in New Hampshire is deteriorating, the health of people in my community could be threatened. 

4. These graphs depict the air-pollution-death rate of every US state and shows whether this air pollution is from in-state or out-of-state sources.

raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the map:  "Death by Air Pollution" by Abigail of Georgia; “Gone With the Wind: Air Pollutant Deaths From Your Neighbors” by Steven of Detroit/Los Angeles; Death in the Air” by Ethan in Ohio; and “No One Is Safe From Air Pollution” by Madison, “The Toll That the Air Is Taking on Your State” by Rigel and “Pollution Is a Pandemic: American People Are Dying From Air Pollution” by Libby, all three from New Hampshire.

 
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Feb. 12 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the map, and a few Stat Nuggets.
 
Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who thinks we can all reduce air pollution by driving less, eating local and turning down the heat and air conditioning, and Kathy Dickensheets, who is enjoying the beautiful snow in Pittsburgh and working to drive much less and reduce air pollution as much as possible.

Hi Math Buddies and Graph Analyzers,
Did you know that we can only talk about correlation when the variables are all quantitative, not categorical?  If any of the variables are categorical, like the state, we can only talk about an association. What type of correlation would you expect between those?

raw_comment:
I noticed that the top graph shows air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents in different shades of purple which represent 1-3 deaths as the purple gets darker. The east coast seems to have more deaths compared to the west coast (except for California)and middle states. The bottom graph shows deaths due to air pollution from out of state compared  in blues and oranges. The darker blue the more in state pollution causing deaths, and the darker orange the more out of state. 

I wonder if both graphs were measured in 2018 or just the top one as stated in the description. I also wonder when most of the country was in lockdown due to the virus in 2020, if the pollution went down, causing the death rates to go down. Lastly, I wonder if pollution will continue to increase, causing more deaths, in these areas or will pollution spread out to more and more areas.

This impacts my community in living in the East coast. As the top graph shows all of the surrounding areas and NJ itself show that there are 3 deaths caused by air pollution for every 10,000 residents. Compared to the rest of the country this should be concerning for all residents. Citizens of NJ and the East Coast should try to find ways to limit this pollution for these death rates to go down.

A headline for these graphs could "Air Pollution Death Rates Across The United States"

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

|---|---|---|

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

raw_comment:
I noticed that states with large and densely populated cities have the most air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents. Overall there are more deaths caused by pollution in the east than in the west. The mid-west seems to have the least number of air pollution deaths. I wonder if there are more deaths just because the population is larger. Are there any cases in which the state population is low, but the death rate by air pollution is high due to other factors such as power plants? I think it's interesting that New York has such high air pollution deaths but mostly out-of-state. Being a very urban state, you would think deaths would be caused more by in-state pollution like California, Illinois, and Pennsylvania. It's also very interesting how states near California don't have high death rates, but the deaths that they do have are mostly caused by in-state pollution. California has both high death rates and much pollution, so I would think that pollution could spread to its surrounding states. I also wonder whom air pollution affects the most - the young, the elderly, or those with respiratory illnesses?

This impacts my community because pollution is a serious issue. It affects the environment and people's lives. One of the factors that cause air pollution is cars, and I think these graphs provide evidence that we need to push for an electric car future, and if not at least hybrid.

A headline could be, "Is the Air We Breathe Killing Us?: Air Pollution Deaths in Each State".

The midwest, which is mostly made up of mountains and forests, has the least amount of pollution as huge cities are not located in this area. I wonder why Washington and Oregon have semi higher numbers of pollution while they are also states made up of mountains and forests. Maybe Seattle causes this pollution or California's pollutions travels upwards to these states. In the second graph, it appears that most states that more highly air polluted states, suffer from higher numbers of pollution deaths out of state. This impacts my community because air pollution deaths in NJ are one of the highest when looking at the map. Because of that, the health of my friends and family can all be impacted by the air pollution present
New Headline: "When Will Clean Air Be Important"

## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that California, Illinois, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Connecticut, New Jersey and New York have the most deaths because of air pollution, which probably means those states have the worst air pollution, States in the south, (excluding Florida and Mississippi) and the northeast (excluding vermont) have bad air quality because of the number of dealths. The same thing goes for parts of the bread basket and rust belt of the state. States out west have the least dealths because of air pollution, so they probably have very clean air. I notice in the second graph that that many states on the west coast have dealths of air pollution because of there own state, whereas many states in the midwest have dealths due to air pollution from other states. Delaware has the most dealths because of air pollution that comes from outside of the state and california has the most dealths because of air pollution that is in the state.
what do you wonder?
I wonder why the west has the cleanest air. I thought Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine would have less dealths because of air pollution. I wonder if the population of a state has to do with the number of dealths, because more populated states seem to have more dealths because of air quality than less populated states.
A title for the graph?
Different regions have different air pollution.

Title: The last breath 
In map number one I notice that the Northern states have higher death rates. I wonder  why California has higher death rates and why it's the only state in the west when most of the high death rates are in the north. In map number two I notice again that in California there are more in state deaths, I wonder why that is. I look back over at the northern states and I notice that most of the dates are out of state unlike California and the western states.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |

raw_comment:
We noticed that the graphs shown represented the number of air pollution deaths per 10,000 people in each state. In the first graph, air pollution deaths are more commonly seen in the East while only a few pop up on the Western coastlines. In the second graph we determined that deaths due to air pollution from in-state are commonly caused by the states along the Western coastlines. 
We wonder why the death per residents were higher on both coasts in the first graph. Also, do the west and east coasts contribute more to plants that cause pollution or are they just a magnet for air pollution? On the second graph, why are more out of state deaths on the eastern side and more in-state deaths happening on the western side?
	Finally, the impact the air pollution has on the entire planet is pretty substantial because it affects the general health of everyone in the world. Air pollution is also a factor for global warming. Our catchy headline is: The toll air pollution takes on life in the U.S.
