raw_comment:
We notice that the western side of the map has much lower death rates than the central and eastern side of the map. We also notice that the central and eastern portions of the map can attribute most of their deaths to out of state sources. Lastly, we notice that the states with higher in state sourced deaths are states that contain a major city. We wonder why Ohio has higher death rates, when it’s population isn’t that big in the first place. Also, we wonder why the Eastern side of the United States has more deaths from air pollution than other parts of the U.S. Is this air pollution particularly from natural causes or factories/carbon emissions? Our most important question is how can we use this information from the graph to further prevent air pollution and the deaths that come from it? This graph has shown us that even in Minnesota, we still have a long way to go before we clear up our pollution. Deaths caused by pollution are high in Minnesota, and we could take some ideas from the states with low amounts of deaths caused by pollution to make our state less polluted. A lot of the areas with high pollution are big cities and since MN has Minneapolis and St. Paul we need to be careful to not end up like the other states with big cities.

With this graph, we can learn more about our community's air quality and learn about other places where we could possibly live in order to avoid death caused by air pollution.

I wonder how much electric cars, especially in major cities, will help combat air pollution? Our graph last week pointed out how much better electric cars are for the environment so I wonder if people were to switch over to electric cars could that solve the air pollution crisis?

This affects my community because I live in NJ, a state with some of the highest air pollution deaths. 3 out of every 10,000 people die from air pollution. This rate is alarming and scary to think about. Air pollution also causes health problems such as asthma and respiratory issues. 

Air Pollution- A Silent Killer

raw_comment:
I notice that for the most part, the highest rates of air pollution deaths are to the mid-East of the country. The west side of the country has significantly lower rates, other than California. In general, I think the more heavily populated the state, the higher the death rate. It's also interesting because looking at the out-of-state vs in-state maps, the areas with the highest death rates actually tended to be more caused by out-of-state pollution. I wonder why the states around California don't have slightly higher death rates. I also wonder why Ohio has higher death rates, when it is not very heavily populated. This impacts me and my community because it shows that areas with bigger populations, or with major cities that cause more traffic, the death rates caused by air pollution is very high. This is concerning because unless we change to electric cars in the near future, the air pollution death rates will likely just continue to increase.

Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea:

Air Pollution Throughout the U.S.

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
Two **choropleth maps** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Vertical small multiples / faceting**: two separate U.S. maps stacked vertically.
- No stacking within a chart.
- Each map uses **state polygons** filled by color to encode a quantitative value.
- State abbreviations are shown as **text labels**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. state | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state polygons on map), text label |
| Air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents | Quantitative | Color/hue intensity on the top choropleth map |
| Deaths due to air pollution from out of state | Quantitative | Color/hue on the bottom choropleth map (blue–orange diverging scale) |
| In-state vs. out-of-state contribution direction | Categorical/ordinal (binary direction around midpoint) | Color side of diverging scale in bottom map (blue = more in-state, orange = more out-of-state, as labeled) |
raw_comment:
Notice:
I notice that the midwest has the least amount of air pollution deaths than any other region in the United States. The entire eastern hemisphere of the United States is affected by more air pollution deaths than the western hemisphere. Additionally, there is a region towards the east coast that is more affected by air pollution deaths than any other region in the United States. This region includes NY, PA, OH, NJ, and CT. The lower map shows that most air pollution within the states comes from out-of state. California and New York, two of the most polluted states, have pollution that comes from different locations. California's pollution comes from in-state, while New York's pollution comes from out-of-state. Thus, the number of air pollution deaths and the location from which the pollution comes are not related. 

What do you wonder?
What is it about the eastern hemisphere that allows for so many more air pollution deaths? Why does it matter where the air pollution is coming from? How can we use the information in the bottom map to combat air pollution within our own states.

Community impact:
I live in a state that is suffers from at least 3 air pollution deaths per 10,000 residents. My state has approximately 8.8 million residents, meaning that there have been about 880 air pollution deaths. The information in the graphs can be used to persuade our governor to make the remediation of pollution a main policy objective.

Headline: The Polluted States of America

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs are maps that show U.S. deaths from air pollution by state and whether the air pollution is generated more in-state or out-of-state.  After all, air pollution does not recognize state boundaries.  Check out your state and the most extreme cases.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex),

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
I noticed that the states with the highest air pollution death count are those with some of the largest cities (New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh, etc.). I also noticed that New Hampshire has a relatively high death count for such a small state.  Lastly, I noticed that most of the states out West have low death counts.
 
2. What do you wonder?

raw_comment:
One thing that I noticed in the first graph is the unit measurement for the graph. The units are deaths per 10,000 residents. Another thing that stuck out to me in the first graph was that the majority of the states on the east coast were darker in shade. More specifically the states in the northeastern part of the U.S. The majority of the states in the center of the U.S. have less deaths per 10,000 residents.
	The second graph is based on in-state and out-of-state residents who have died due to air pollution. In this graph, I noticed that a lot of the deaths in the northeastern states that had more deaths in the first graph, have more out of state deaths. Most of South Dakota’s deaths are from out of state. 
	Some questions I have for the first graph are: “Why are most of the darker states in the West Coast and in the northeastern corner?” “What is causing these states to have more deaths due to air pollution?” Some questions I have for the second graph are: “Why are the majority of South Dakota’s deaths out of state?” "Why do the west coast states not change to out of state like the northeastern states are?”
	I have lived my entire life in Iowa. They are in the 1-2 range of deaths per 10,000 and the majority of their deaths come from out of state. Iowa also is not the most populated state, so their deaths per state is quite low.
	I think that a catchy headline for these maps would be, “More Populated Areas, More Air Pollution Deaths”.

raw_comment:
I notice that in the air pollution deaths graph that the states with the most amount of deaths are some of the ones with the most populated cities like California, Illinois, and New York. I also notice that Pennsylvania is one of those states that has the most amount of air pollution deaths and that state has a large coal industry which could be a factor to their amount of pollution. 

I wonder why South Dakota, Delaware, and Rhode Island have the most deaths from air pollution in-state? They aren’t very populated so I wonder what they are doing in their states to create that much air pollution.

This impacts me and my community because air pollution is dangerous and is everywhere. The graphs show the severity of pollution and the fact that even if it isn’t coming from your state, it can still affect it.These graphs also help bring attention to the problem and hope for changes to be made.

After looking closely at the graph above, answer these four questions:

What do you notice?

31/48 of the states had the majority of their deaths caused by air pollution from outside or neighboring states. 
States notorious for their pollution: Pennsylvania, California, Texas had neighboring states with death rates similar to theirs. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder if we mapped the states by their industry (found using GDP) would we find coal and oil production for CA, PA and TX the main culprits?

How many non-human deaths occur for the same reason? 
How many of our birds, fish and other wildlife are affected by these pollutants?

What impact does this have on you and your community?

Passing legislation for air filtration, pollution reduction, and carbon capture in your state may not be enough. Neighboring states would have to do the same in order to significantly drop death rates nation and worldwide.


What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

Gone With the Wind; Air Pollutant Deaths from Your Neighbors

raw_comment:
I notice that 3 of the states with the most premature deaths due to air pollution are homes to 3 of the biggest cities in the country (California/Los Angeles, Illinois/Chicago, and New York/New York City). If we look at lower populated states, it is evident that there is much less air pollution. This could suggest that highly populated regions often have a negative impact on air quality. 
Looking at the second display, I wonder why states like South Dakota, Rhode Island, and Delaware have the most out of state deaths due to air pollution. Compared to other larger states, these 3 states typically aren’t the most popular places to be. There are fewer residential areas, and less transportation in general, so I find it confusing that these 3 states have the most out of state deaths due to air pollution.
 

This impacts me and my community because air quality is a public health concern, and this graph shows us which states need to make the most changes to their consumption of fuels, which emit pollutants.

Headline: “The Fatal Consequences of Excessive Fuel Consumption”

I see that the states with the most air pollution deaths in the first graph are the more likely in the east and west coasts while the Midwest is a lot less likely. I wonder as to why it is that the east and west coast experiences more premature deaths from air pollution in comparison to the Midwest. My assumption is that since that the east and west coast contain more densely populated cities, it makes sense that those locations are where there are more factories because that is where the profit is. Since that the Midwest is extremely spread out, there are less factories over there that omit air pollution, thus decreasing premature deaths. This impacts my community in a negative way because I do live in a densely populated area with a lot of darker shaded regions in the Northeast. It kind of worries me because our children are more likely to be affected by air pollution than children that are born in the Midwest. It makes me hope that our state has regulations and sees that this is a growing issue before it is too late. Potential headline: "Air Pollution: Which States are More Affected?"

This impacts my community and me by reinforcing the idea that pollution damages the immediate vicinity of the source, as well as surrounding areas that are hundreds of miles away. 
4. “The Fatal Ramifications of Air Pollution.”

What do you notice?

I notice that some of the darker states, i.e. Illinois, California, and New York, each contain some of the biggest cities in the country. I believe this would heavily contribute to more air pollution from transportation/car emissions in these highly populated urban areas. On the contrary, states like Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho have low rates of air pollution deaths that could be from the lack of urbanization and greater presence of open land, flora, and natural landscapes.  

What do you wonder?

The second graph makes me ask a lot of questions. Why does a state like South Dakota have the most out-of-state air pollution deaths? Does it have to do with the underground oil pipeline in North Dakota? Also, let’s look at year-round warmer states like Texas and Florida. Do they have high in-state causes due to the constant use of air conditioners to keep families cool?

What impact does this have on you and your community?

This impacts my community greatly because my family currently lives in Illinois, which is one of the states that has the highest air pollution deaths in the country. This worries me for my parents, my siblings, and myself considering we grew up there for most of our lives. This makes me more aware of the great issue of air pollution that we may not be able to see or feel in our day-to-day lives.

What’s going on in these maps? Write a catchy headline that captures the maps’ main idea.

The Sad Truth about Air Pollution
